To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we found corticomuscular coupling in the 6-15 Hz frequency band in four of the six patients and that it was focal on the primary motor area and distributed somatotopic.
the 6-15 Hz corticomuscular coherences in the PT are due to a direct cortical contribution to the generation of PT, rather than a feedback of the mechanical tremor to the motor cortex.
the corticomuscular 6-15 Hz coherence reflects a corticomotor transmission rather than a feedback from the periphery.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of the generation and propagation of tremor.
the role of the central nervous system in physiologic tremors.
the question of how the brain controls the movements of the body.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cortical contribution is a significant component in the generation of tremor and that the cortical oscillation in the 6-15 Hz band is a cortical contribution to tremor generation.
the cortex is not the only source of the physiologic tremors, but that it contributes to it.
cortical networks are indeed involved in the generation and control of tremor, but that the exact role of the cortex is still unclear and needs further investigation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the central component in physiologic tremors is generated in the primary motor cortex and that it is transmitted through fast pyramidal systems to the muscle.
the central component of physiologic hand tremor is generated by cortical networks, which is supported by a significant coherence between epicortical and electromyographic recordings.
the central component of physiologic (or postural) tremor is generated by cortical networks and is transmitted via fast pyramidal tracts to the muscles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cortex plays an important role in physiologic tremors.
the central component of PT is not a simple peripheral oscillation but is generated by central oscillators.
the central component of physiologic oscillations can be generated by cortical networks and that the frequency of this oscillation can be modulated by cortical activity.
